inputs.need:
I am an anaesthetist and the clinical lead for our day surgery unit, which does about 6,000 adult procedures a year in gynaecology, orthopaedics, general surgery and ENT. Two years ago we adopted a risk-tailored protocol for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting: patients are scored with a simple four-factor risk score and should receive one, two or three antiemetic agents depending on the score. Our recovery nurses keep a nausea log, and it shows that about one patient in eight still needs a rescue antiemetic, and nausea is the commonest reason for an unplanned overnight stay. When I look at individual cases, many seem not to have had the prophylaxis the protocol asks for, but I only see the ones that go wrong.

We want to do a case-control study: take patients who needed rescue treatment for nausea or vomiting in recovery or whose discharge was delayed by it, compare them with patients from the same operating lists who did not, and check in the anaesthetic record whether prophylaxis matched the protocol for their risk score. The drug section of the anaesthetic record is on paper, so every record has to be read by hand, which is why we cannot look at everyone. I would like to know whether patients who received less prophylaxis than the protocol recommends are more likely to need rescue treatment, and whether giving more than recommended causes sedation that delays discharge.

I need help defining cases and controls, deciding how many records we need to read, and handling the fact that sicker patients and longer operations may get more prophylaxis anyway.
localFacts: The day surgery unit performed about 6,000 adult procedures last year; the recovery nausea log recorded a rescue antiemetic for 742 patients.
The drug section of the anaesthetic record is on paper and is scanned into the hospital record after discharge.
The health records department approved access to scanned anaesthetic records for this project on 2026-09-09 (approval HR-2026-118).
No research ethics board application has been submitted yet.

response.subtitle: Case-control study of under- and over-prophylaxis
response.statement: In a day surgery unit of about 6,000 adult procedures a year, about one patient in eight needs a rescue antiemetic in recovery and nausea is the commonest reason for unplanned overnight stays, two years after a risk-tailored prophylaxis protocol was adopted. response.patientCenteredGoal: Every patient receives the prophylaxis their risk calls for and goes home on the day of surgery without nausea or sedation holding them back.

records.title: Adherence to risk-tailored antiemetic prophylaxis in ambulatory surgery: an observational study
records.authors: Kowalski-Mensah J, Oduya-Bright L, Svensson-Park A
records.abstract: We compared the antiemetic prophylaxis given with that recommended by a risk-tailored protocol in consecutive adults undergoing ambulatory surgery at two hospitals. Across 3,400 ambulatory surgery patients, prophylaxis matched the risk-tailored protocol in 52 percent. Under-prophylaxis was most common in patients with the highest risk scores, who received fewer agents than recommended in 38 percent of cases, while over-prophylaxis was most common in low-risk patients. Adherence varied more between anaesthetists than between surgical specialties. Risk scores were reconstructed from records, which may have misclassified some patients. A protocol alone did not ensure that prophylaxis matched risk.

records.title: Under-prophylaxis and nausea or vomiting requiring rescue treatment after day surgery: a case-control analysis
records.abstract: We identified 214 day surgery patients who needed rescue antiemetic treatment in recovery and 428 controls from the same operating lists, and read their anaesthetic records to classify prophylaxis against the unit protocol. Under-prophylaxis was associated with nausea or vomiting requiring rescue treatment (adjusted odds ratio 1.8, 95 percent CI 1.2 to 2.7) after adjustment for risk score, duration of surgery and opioid dose. Over-prophylaxis was not associated with fewer rescue treatments. Record readers were not blinded to case status, and the protocol changed during the study period. The findings support checking adherence as a target for improvement.

records.title: Recovery unit nausea logs as a source of outcome data: agreement with nurse observation
records.abstract: We compared entries in a recovery unit nausea log with direct observation by research nurses for 480 adults after day surgery. Recovery unit nausea logs captured 87 percent of rescue antiemetic treatments seen by nurse observers, and almost all missed entries occurred during busy periods at the end of the day. Nausea that did not lead to treatment was captured far less reliably. Entries were accurate for the drug and the time given. The log is a reasonable source for rescue treatment as an outcome but not for nausea severity. The study took place in one unit with an established logging culture.

records.title: Risk-tailored versus fixed antiemetic prophylaxis for adults having surgery: a review of comparative studies
records.authors: Delacroix-Osei M, Lindgren-Adeyemi S, Tanaka-Frost E, Holloway-Nkemelu B
records.abstract: We reviewed 19 comparative studies of risk-tailored and fixed antiemetic prophylaxis in adults having surgery under general anaesthesia. Risk-tailored prophylaxis reduced the incidence of nausea and vomiting in high-risk patients compared with fixed single-agent regimens, while low-risk patients received fewer drugs with similar outcomes. Benefits depended on adherence, which was reported in only seven studies and was often below 60 percent. Few studies reported discharge outcomes after day surgery. Most studies were before-after comparisons with moderate to high risk of bias, and definitions of nausea and vomiting varied widely.

records.title: Unplanned overnight admission after day surgery: causes and the contribution of nausea and vomiting
records.abstract: We reviewed all unplanned overnight admissions after day surgery in three units over one year. Of 312 unplanned admissions, 31 percent were attributed to nausea and vomiting, 24 percent to pain and 18 percent to surgical complications. Admissions for nausea were more common after gynaecological laparoscopy and in patients who received opioids in recovery. Units differed in how they recorded the reason for admission, and the attribution was made by the discharging nurse. Reducing nausea and vomiting could reduce unplanned admissions substantially, but the proportion depends on local case mix.

records.title: Over-prophylaxis with antiemetics and sedation delaying discharge after day surgery
records.abstract: We examined whether giving more antiemetic agents than recommended by the risk score affected recovery after day surgery in 1,860 adults. Giving more antiemetic agents than the risk score indicated was associated with sedation that delayed discharge in 6 percent of patients, compared with 2 percent of patients whose prophylaxis matched the score. The difference was largest when a sedating antihistamine was added. Rescue treatment rates were similar in the two groups. The analysis could not fully separate the effect of extra antiemetics from that of the conditions that prompted anaesthetists to give them.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Adherence to risk-tailored prophylaxis was about half in one large study, with high-risk patients under-treated most often. A case-control analysis found under-prophylaxis associated with rescue treatment, and a recovery nausea log captured most rescue treatments, which makes rescue treatment a workable case definition. Over-prophylaxis was associated with sedation delaying discharge rather than fewer rescue treatments. Nausea caused about a third of unplanned admissions in three units. The evidence supports a local case-control study with record reading, with separate attention to over-prophylaxis.
response.gradeRationale: Observational studies with confounding by indication and unblinded record reading; consistent in direction.

response.reading: Prophylaxis sits between the risk score and two opposite harms: under-prophylaxis leading to rescue treatment (c2) and over-prophylaxis leading to sedation and delayed discharge (c4). Adherence is likely to be partial (c1). The recovery log defines cases reliably enough (c3), while the paper drug record limits how many patients can be examined, which favours sampling cases and controls. Longer operations, opioids and sicker patients push toward both more prophylaxis and more nausea, which is the main confounding path.

response.overview: Case-control study of adults who had day surgery between January 2025 and June 2026, with cases from the recovery nausea log and two controls per case from the same operating lists, classifying prophylaxis against the risk-tailored protocol from scanned anaesthetic records.

Readers see the drug section before the recovery section, so exposure is classified before case status is visible where the scan order allows.

response.designSummary: Case-control study with two controls per case from the same operating list; conditional logistic regression.
response.sampleSize: With matched prophylaxis in about 55 percent of controls (planning value near the 52 percent reported elsewhere) and an odds ratio of 0.6 for matched prophylaxis compared with under-prophylaxis, 80 percent power at two-sided alpha 0.05 with two controls per case needs about 182 cases and 364 controls, 546 records in all. The nausea log recorded 742 rescue treatments last year, so about nine months of lists supply enough cases; the 18-month window allows cases to be sampled at random. Reading 546 records at about six minutes each takes about 55 hours, within the 60 hours available.
response.primaryAnalysis: Conditional logistic regression of case status on prophylaxis category (under, matched, over; matched as reference) adjusted for risk score, duration of surgery and opioid dose, reporting odds ratios with 95 percent confidence intervals.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Logistic regression of sedation delaying discharge on over-prophylaxis among all sampled patients, adjusted for the same variables; adherence among controls with its interval; agreement between the two readers (kappa) on exposure category.
response.missingData: A missing risk score is reconstructed from recorded factors and flagged; if factors are missing too, the record is kept with a missing-score category and a sensitivity analysis excludes it.
response.multiplicity: One primary contrast (under versus matched); secondary analyses reported with intervals and labelled as secondary.
response.software: R with the survival package for conditional logistic regression; extraction form and analysis code archived before reading starts.
overfittingGuards: Three adjustment variables fixed before extraction

response.effectiveness: The study is useful if it shows whether adherence support should be the unit's next improvement target.

response.costs: Fellow time within training allowances; no other costs.

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am an anaesthetist and the clinical lead for our day surgery unit, which does about 6,000 adult procedures a year in gynaecology, orthopaedics, general surgery and ENT. Two years ago we adopted a risk-tailored protocol for preventing postoperative nausea and vomiting: patients are scored with a simple four-factor risk score and should receive one, two or three antiemetic agents depending on the score. Our recovery nurses keep a nausea log, and it shows that about one patient in eight still needs a rescue antiemetic, and nausea is the commonest reason for an unplanned overnight stay. When I look at individual cases, many seem not to have had the prophylaxis the protocol asks for, but I only see the ones that go wrong.

We want to do a case-control study: take patients who needed rescue treatment for nausea or vomiting in recovery or whose discharge was delayed by it, compare them with patients from the same operating lists who did not, and check in the anaesthetic record whether prophylaxis matched the protocol for their risk score. The drug section of the anaesthetic record is on paper, so every record has to be read by hand, which is why we cannot look at everyone. I would like to know whether patients who received less prophylaxis than the protocol recommends are more likely to need rescue treatment, and whether giving more than recommended causes sedation that delays discharge.

I need help defining cases and controls, deciding how many records we need to read, and handling the fact that sicker patients and longer operations may get more prophylaxis anyway.
